speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: During the debate on the Workplace Fairness Bill earlier this year, brother Heng Chee How emphasised how an ageing population is a major challenge for global economies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Through my engagements with union leaders as well as individuals and workers of different segments and in particular, recently, of senior workers, I have also heard concerns from our seniors about ageism in hiring, in training and in promotion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I have covered some of these topics in the Motion of Thanks debate this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Globally, we also see that age discrimination at workplaces has led to significant legal consequences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In the United States, IBM faced lawsuits over layoffs since 2016 that allegedly targeted older workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: More recently, IKEA settled five lawsuits for passing over older workers for promotions and unfairly labelling them as lacking potential.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For senior workers, discrimination often compounds existing anxieties, including their job security, re-employment or their skills relevance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is therefore vital to provide a trusted and accessible avenue for redress, giving them confidence and dignity at work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Therefore, I want to thank the Government for working closely with the tripartite partners to design the dispute resolution process that ensures that workers, including our senior workers, have a fair, accessible and effective pathway to their WFA claims.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As the executive secretary of SISEU, I see our union leaders and our industrial relations officers working tirelessly to support our members.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Last year, SISEU handled over 100 individual grievances, including professionals, managers and executives (PMEs) and members from non-unionised firms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Most were resolved amicably, at the union level, through mediation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: SISEU supported a wrongful dismissal case involving a PME in his mid-40s, terminated with one month's notice, despite a satisfactory performance and without clear explanation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Age discrimination in the workplace is often subtle and difficult to detect, as it can take the form of indirect practices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: On the ground, it is not uncommon to hear that when companies downsize, older workers are often the first to be let go.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: SISEU highlighted a case where a company asked employees nearing retirement age to resign voluntarily or risk losing medical benefits, only to replace them with new younger workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: With union intervention, the company eventually recognised the violation and took corrective actions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While this may have stemmed from a new management unfamiliar with local norms, it underscores how similar cases and practices could be adopted elsewhere, whether they are intentional or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As Mr Lee Kuan Yew puts it, "Self-respect is what our trade unions have and will give to our workers, that protection for a man's right to his own dignity." This Bill puts that principle into action.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Senior workers now have stronger legal protection against disguised bias, where NTUC and our unions can better represent workers in resolving disputes and restoring this important dignity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Before any dispute escalates to ECT, NTUC also provides accessible support for our members.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our LawWorks legal clinics, through our partnership with Pro Bono SG and the network of volunteer lawyers, offer complementary basic legal advice to members, including for employment- and workplace-related matters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I know that Member He Ting Ru mentioned that the website of Pro Bono SG did not indicate that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We will check on the website, but in practice, on the ground, we see the majority of cases coming to LawWorks are personal workplace- and employment-related cases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We will similarly extend this support and this legal claim to provide advice to members for discrimination cases under the WFA as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For members in unionised companies, they can, in addition to the legal clinics, continue to rely on our industrial relation officers who are well-versed with the Industrial Relations Act and workplace matters and equipped to represent our workers to the best of our ability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I also want to respond to Member Shawn Loh's question whether NTUC will support non-members of NTUC to join NTUC in order to obtain support from us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My response is that all workers should join NTUC today and not wait until they need support from us, because we are here to support every worker and every worker is important to us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Beyond discrimination at work, many senior workers report applying for numerous jobs but receiving silent rejection.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In my earlier Motion of Thanks speech, I shared one such real-life story and also urged employers to better recognise their expertise accumulated from years of experience of our senior workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As recruitment becomes increasingly digital, we must also guard against age bias in artificial intelligence (AI)-based hiring tools.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These include working with tripartite partners to develop fair hiring standards for the use of AI and to equip our HR practitioners with the right skills and tools to detect and mitigate algorithmic bias.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Given the varied nature of grievance cases, the Government should actively collect data and conduct regular review of the legislation in collaboration with tripartite partners to ensure that it remains responsive to the evolving societal norms and workforce demographics.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And one suggestion I want to offer here is to review the ECT limit for all other workforce or workplace claims.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is especially if the expanded ECT for WFA claims works well going forward.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the Workplace Fairness Act is crucial for safeguarding the rights and dignity of senior workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This Act will ensure that senior workers have an avenue for redress, helping them regain dignity and confidence in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Workplace Fairness Act and the Workplace Fairness (Dispute Resolution) Bill, through the Judge-led Employment Claims Tribunal with its mediation-first approach without high legal costs, ensure that all workers, including seniors, have a fair, accessible and effective pathway for their WFA claims.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Here, I would like to thank MOM and our tripartite partners for their attention to maintaining workplace fairness, particularly their focus on seniors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As the saying goes: "The seniors are like jade; they are treasures of the nation." In this digital age, we need to continue supporting seniors to remain actively engaged in work and social environments, enabling them to enjoy their golden years with dignity and confidence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: (In English): In closing, Mr Speaker, this Bill gives senior workers stronger protection, along with better access to union representation through the expanded claims framework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is a significant step forward in ensuring fair treatment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Beyond legal protections, we must build workplace cultures that respect and empower workers of all ages, where experience is seen as an asset, not a liability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is a key priority of tripartite partners under the Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment, which I co-chair.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as I reviewed this Bill, I found myself thinking not just about the legal frameworks and tribunal procedures outlined in its pages, but also people from all walks of life who will need to navigate these systems to seek justice.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Among these will be persons with disabilities and special needs, who most often draw the shortest end of the stick.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, I rise in strong support of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I also rise to ask four questions that might help this legislation truly deliver fairness for persons with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But architecture must be accompanied with the frameworks to ensure that those who need access to its protection can enter.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He had been working in a professional services firm when he began experiencing what he believed was discrimination related to his disability.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When he tried to raise his concerns through his company's grievance process, he found the procedures overwhelming.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The internal HR process required him to navigate dense policy documents he found difficult to understand.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When he attended meetings with HR representatives, they spoke rapidly using corporate jargon and expected immediate verbal responses: something extremely challenging for him as an autistic person who needs time to process information.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My second recommendation addresses a fundamental asymmetry of power that persons with disabilities face in dispute resolution.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill wisely provides for representation at mediation sessions.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Employers who are corporate bodies may be represented by officers or employees.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During a particularly stressful period at work, my resident was required to participate in work calls with IT colleagues that his autism job coach from the Autism Resource Centre had explicitly recommended he be excluded from, or at minimum, that someone always accompany him during such interactions.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These calls were neurologically incompatible for him – they were complex, unstructured, unpredictable, filled with incomplete information and confusing technical jargon.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They triggered intense stress and made him feel psychologically unsafe.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Despite this professional recommendation for a reasonable accommodation, business needs overrode the advice.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During one exceptionally traumatic call that pushed him near to an autistic meltdown, my resident made a comment expressing his extreme distress.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But in the debrief meeting that followed, his managers ignored his distress entirely and focused solely on what they deemed "unprofessional behaviour".

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: His managers even threatened to negatively impact his performance appraisal, a form of indirect discrimination since his reactions were directly related to his disability, until a more senior leader intervened.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Sitting across from corporate representatives, he would have difficulty articulating the nuanced context of his disability – why being corrected and reprimanded for a disability-related reaction constitutes harassment, why the denial of recommended accommodations created the conditions for the incident and why threatening his performance appraisal for needing accommodations is discriminatory.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These organisations understand the unique challenges persons with disabilities face.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They can help persons with disabilities prepare their cases, organise their evidence and communicate their experiences differently.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They can identify when workplace "performance issues" are actually disability discrimination disguised as legitimate business decisions.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill already contemplates that unions can represent parties in dispute resolution but union representatives, while skilled in employment matters, may not have specialised training in disability issues.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Compliance with WCAG means ensuring that online portals work with screen readers for persons with visual impairments.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It means providing text alternatives for all images and charts.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It means ensuring sufficient colour contrast for persons with low vision or colour blindness.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It means designing forms that are navigable by keyboard for persons with mobility limitations.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It means using clear, simple language for persons with intellectual or cognitive disabilities.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would go a long, long way in ensuring that the information and protection provided by the Bill and its guidelines are available to all.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And when we design evidence rules that account for the realities of how discrimination operates, we ensure that persons with disabilities do not face impossible burdens when asserting their rights.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A workplace fairness system that works for persons with disabilities is a system that works for everyone.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We build it for those who need it most – persons who use wheelchairs – but once it is there, it helps everyone: parents with strollers, delivery riders, the elderly.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Likewise, when we design our workplace systems to include persons with disabilities, we build a Singapore that is more humane and ultimately, more just for all.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And when Singapore proves that every person, regardless of ability, can access justice with dignity, we will have built not just fairer workplaces, but a more compassionate nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In today's context, whereby labour is globally mobile and the workplace has essentially become borderless, the competition between economies for jobs is now much more intense.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a business-friendly environment, we have to understand that employers need clarity, flexibility and certainty so that they can continue to innovate and compete without undue fear of litigation or disruption.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employees will have more certainty and confidence that decisions around hiring, promotion, training and termination will be based on merit.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Those who believe they have been unfairly treated now have clearer and more accessible recourse avenues.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The internal grievance process helps ensure that matters can be raised within the firm.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is also in line with what is commonly known as "not burning bridges".

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that employers will view this new development positively and understand that the legislation is helping them to build stronger teams and healthier, more engaged workplaces.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the certainty offered by this piece of legislation, employers now have a clearer framework for setting up grievance mechanisms, conducting fair employment practices, understanding what constitutes adverse employment decisions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the Bill prioritises internal resolution and mediation, employers have the opportunity to resolve disputes internally or at early stages rather than getting right into expensive, possibly protracted litigation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This helps preserve employer-employee relationships, maintain morale and reduce the risk of reputational damage.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I wanted to just highlight some potential practicalities that may be faced by employees and employers as this is being rolled out.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To realise the full potential of this Bill, we need to address the following issues.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, employees and jobseekers should be aware of their rights and the processes available to them and feel empowered to raise concerns without fear of retaliation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employees may not be aware of their rights or may be unfamiliar with the process.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the Ministry be planning to raise their awareness and educate them on the steps they need to take, such as keeping records and evidence of discriminatory practices?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Employees and jobseekers should be aware of their rights and the processes available to them, and feel empowered to raise concerns without fear of retaliation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employees may not be aware of their rights or may be unfamiliar with the process.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the Ministry be planning to raise their awareness and educate them on the steps they need to take, such as keeping records and evidence of discriminatory practices?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Second, tripartite partners, unions, employer associations, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM), TAFEP should continue their education and outreach to ensure that the transition is smooth and that smaller firms are supported.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, employers should proactively review and strengthen their internal grievance handling procedures, provide training for managers and staff, and encourage a culture of openness and fairness.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I know that this does not happen overnight, but it is in the interests of the company to do so.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, while the Bill aims to prevent abuse of the system, the safeguards for employers against unmerited claims could be a barrier to employees seeking redress.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some employees may be worried that they will have to go through a longer and more onerous process than simply sending a complaint to the authorities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is the Ministry's assessment of this issue?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I urge businesses to view this legislation as an opportunity, not simply as a compliance burden, but as a catalyst for better workplaces, where employees feel respected and empowered, where both sides can focus on what matters most and that is doing good work together.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By giving statutory force to fair employment principles, this Bill reinforces Singapore's commitment to an inclusive, rules-based labour market where both employers and employees can operate with confidence.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we implement this framework, I would like to raise several points for clarification and recommendations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This aligns with our tripartite approach of resolving conflicts through dialogue and conciliation rather than confrontation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Workers without HR support or legal literacy must feel safe in coming forward.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As TAFEP transitions from advisory to enforcement, clear communication is critical so that everyone understands where to go, what to do and what to expect when a dispute arises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, while the Bill emphasises the importance of internal resolution, we must recognise that unequal power dynamics persist in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employees may feel intimidated, uncertain, or afraid of retaliation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And where harm or undue pressure is likely, could the Bill allow employees to proceed directly to mediation?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would protect vulnerable workers while preserving fair and proportionate resolution.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, employers bear the responsibility to uphold fair practices and cooperate fully with investigations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yet, many SMEs may lack the HR capacity to meet these new statutory expectations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our collective goal must be to prevent disputes before they even arise.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To achieve this, we need to strengthen HR capabilities across all enterprises, ensuring practices are professional, transparent and consistently applied.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this regard, promotion and appraisal process deserves special attention.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These decisions are often subjective and yet they have profound implications for employee morale, retention and progression.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To reduce misunderstanding and build trust, companies, especially SMEs, should be encouraged to review and clarify their performance appraisal and promotion criteria, ensuring that they are fair, evidence-based and relevant to their business context.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, could TAFEP or MOM provide advisory resources, templates or capability programmes to help companies design fair and defensible HR frameworks aligned with the intent and spirit of this Bill?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fourth, we must also guard against frivolous claims.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, some employees may allege discrimination over return-to-office policies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The system must remain balanced, protecting genuine cases, but preventing misuse.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clear definitions and examples of discrimination will give both employers and employees the confidence to act fairly and reasonably.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fifth, where discrimination is proven, tribunals may order compensation or reinstatement.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill will expand the roles of MOM and TAFEP in mediation and enforcement.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What resources will be provided to ensure timely resolution and consistent outcomes, because predictability builds confidence for both employers and employees?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, legislation can set the rules, but it cannot change culture alone.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers, especially SMEs, need guidance to put these new requirements into practice.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through workshops, toolkits and real examples, they can help both employers and employees understand their responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because fairness should not just be a legal requirement, it should be a shared workplace value.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My clarifications are made in the spirit of strengthening its implementation, ensuring that both employers and employees can operate in a system that is fair, balanced and trusted by all.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It represents one of the most structured and progressive statutory frameworks of its kind in our region in past.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For me personally, this has been a long-awaited milestone.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ten years ago, in my maiden speech, I spoke about fair employment practices and the need for enhanced anti-discrimination protections.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Other MPs have also spoken about it over the years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is more than a legal reform; it is a social compact for the future of work in Singapore, one that balances fairness, accountability and economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore's approach, grounded in tripartism and trust between Government, unions and employers, makes this framework uniquely Singaporean and regionally possibly distinctive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He mentioned about it being scheduled by end of 2027.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what I want to reiterate here is the fact that for employers to plan ahead, a clear timeline and transparent update ahead of implementation will be useful, especially in the current economic and trading environment that we are seeing globally.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My question, therefore, on TAFEP, would be, as Minister Tan has shared earlier, he has elaborated in his opening speech about the role that TAFEP will play.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My question is, after hearing what Minister Tan has asked, is given the range of work to be done by TAFEP, would TAFEP's budget and resources be scaled up or down, or maintained, following the implementation of the WFA?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think TAFEP will play a significant role, going forward, from what I have heard from Minister Tan, given the expectations also from the Members in the Chamber, especially in the need to simplify things and in particular, possibly making things in vernacular so that our employees can understand it further, including employers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second point, Mr Speaker, is on the claims procedure and internal grievance handling processes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I understand it, an aggrieved individual would need to go through three sequential stages to pursue a claim against an employer or firm.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, the employee must resort to the firm's internal grievance handling process at the first instance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would there be minimum standards that such internal processes would have to meet and would they be subject to audit by supervising agencies?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think this is the first hurdle before things get progressive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is important, especially if you are also subjecting an individual who is complaining about a discriminatory decision not to hire him or her under section 5 of the WFA.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Unlike individuals complaining about discriminatory employment decisions during employment, or in respect of dismissal, retrenchment or termination, such an individual would not have signed a contract with the firm where he or she might have agreed to the firm's internal grievance handling process.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In a similar vein, would the Ministry and/or its agencies roll out training on how to institute or improve an acceptable grievance handling process before the WFA goes live, and as mentioned, end 2027 – so, we still have a few years to go before then.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think many in this room have shared about their concerns on the mediation front.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, an aggrieved individual would have to attempt mediation as a precondition to filing a claim against the employer or firm.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill provides that this will be evidenced by a "claim referral certificate", issued by an approved mediator if the dispute cannot be settled by mediation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the duration that the individual has to commence a claim after receiving a "claim referral certificate"?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will each certificate stipulate a bespoke time limit for that particular claim to be brought in the High Court or the ECT?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If so, what should an individual claimant do if his or her "claim referral certificate" lapses or expires?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A bit of a technical question that I have.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, we must have mediators, if other Members have spoken, mediators who are sensitive to the context of our unique system, emphasising tripartism and harmonious labour relations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the size of the pool of approved mediators that will be maintained?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Practising lawyers, HR specialists or Public Service officers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the consequence if a claimant is out of time?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is any and all recourse precluded, such that the claimant cannot pursue the workplace fairness claim in mediation or in Court?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe this has been raised by others as well before me.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It also appears difficult for a claimant to determine the expiry of the time bar if the employer does not give notice of the employment decision.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the new section 36E, how does the Ministry expect the time bars in limbs (2)(b) and (3)(b) to work?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The prescribed time bars also make reasonable concessions for pregnant individuals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In relation to the new section 36E(4)(a) of the Bill, must there be formal certification of pregnancy or is a clinical diagnosis by a registered medical practitioner enough?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is it truly the intent to subject pregnant women, for example, to dispute resolution under the WFA, prior to the end of their confinement, just because they only got their pregnancy confirmed by a doctor after the employer's alleged discriminatory dismissal or termination?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   I would like to state for the record my appreciation to the Government for the amendments to the Workplace Fairness Act that aim to protect Singapore workers from any form of discrimination.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is in line with the ECT's objective to maintain a simple, personal and judge-led process.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, I would like to ask — has any satisfaction survey or study ever been conducted on individuals and employers regarding the process and outcomes of ECT proceedings, given that legal representation is generally not permitted?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This situation could create an inequality of opportunity, as companies, partnerships or organisations can still be represented by in-house counsel who are their full-time officers or employees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that this is the current rule for ECT proceedings.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, does the Ministry have data on how many cases involve employers being represented by full-time in-house lawyers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To maintain the principle of equality of arms, could aggrieved individuals be permitted to be accompanied by lawyer friends during mediation sessions or tribunal proceedings — provided that the lawyer does not act as their legal representative?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If so, I hope this matter can be clarified in the subsidiary legislation to be introduced under Section 36I(3) in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This principle of equality also exists in other regulations, where employers may only be represented by trade union representatives if workers are also represented by their own union.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, I would like to seek a clarification — must workers actually have union representation, or is it enough that they are eligible for union representation in order to allow employers to also have union representatives?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): The need for legal representation is underscored by the need to navigate alternative avenues of recourse for unfair dismissal, such as bringing a claim in the Industrial Arbitration Court or making representations to the Minister under the Industrial Relations Act 1960 or the Retirement and Re-employment Act 1993.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The new sections 36L and 36M deal with this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From my layman reading, it appears that you cannot commence a WFA claim after making representations to the Minister, but you can maintain both if you commence the WFA claim first before making representations to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How practical is such an option for reinstatement, especially when trust and confidence would have broken down between the employer and the employee?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From past cases which have been determined by the ECT or dealt with by the TADM, may I know how many cases actually saw the reinstatement and re-establishment of the employer-employee relationship at the end of the process?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And what proportion of these were voluntarily agreed by the parties and how many were foisted on the parties by an order?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The proposed additions to the WFA and the Employment Claims Act 2016 also suggest, but do not detail, that a monetary limit will be set for claims of discriminatory hiring under section 5(1) of WFA.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the rationale for such a claim limit when no similar limit is suggested for discriminatory employment decisions during employment or in respect of termination?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will there be one limit or multiple limits for different scenarios?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another concern is that it may be difficult to quantify the precise loss or damages that flow from a discriminatory employment decision.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, what would be the precise loss for someone who was passed over for a promotion because of a protected characteristic, besides any bonus or pay increment that he or she should have gotten?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even for the pay increment, what is the number of months or years that should be used to calculate the total loss?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are a few ways that we can possibly fill this gap, based on existing solutions used elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One, we can stipulate a default amount or rate of statutory damages where actual loss need not be proven, as already done for intellectual property infringement under the Trade Marks Act or Copyright Act.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Two, we can allow the ECT or Court to appoint a single joint expert to determine damages if a discriminatory decision is established.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Related to this is another suggestion that I raised when we debated the first part of WFA back in January 2025.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But for now, I thank MOM for their immense work in giving Singapore our own version of anti-discrimination laws which have been promulgated in most developed countries and which I have had to cite in my 2019 and 2021 Adjournment Motions on fair employment practices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, we have our own, if passed, to operate and improve in years to come for the benefit of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In that debate, I shared my own personal experience of encountering racial prejudice in the workplace and how, while the situation has improved significantly over the years, workplace discrimination remains a concern for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It can be subtle, in hiring decisions, in career progression opportunities or in the way performance feedback is given.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It can appear in informal networks, in workplace culture or in the unconscious biasness that shape decisions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These experiences may not always make the news, but for the individuals involved, they can be deeply painful and affect their dignity and confidence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That is why the Workplace Fairness Legislation is important.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Together with the Workplace Fairness (Dispute Resolution) Bill before us today, it sends a strong signal of our national commitment to fairness, respect and equal opportunity for all workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The framework recognises that while legal redress is important, the best outcome is not always found in the courtroom.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: However, for the legislation to be truly effective, most disputes should ideally be resolved within the first two steps: the internal grievances process and mediation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If every case goes straight to adjudication, we risk fracturing workplaces, relationships and creating an adversarial climate that benefits no one.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Hence, my clarifications today will focus on how we can strengthen these first two steps to make them more accessible, fair and effective for both employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Having such data, even in aggregate, would allow us to monitor trends, identify common types of discrimination and understand which industries or sectors are most affected.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For instance, are most cases related to gender, age, race or disability?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Are they concentrated in certain job functions or company sizes?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Having this insight will help us to fine-tune future policies and training resources.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It would also be useful to understand how many of these cases were successfully resolved at the internal or mediation stage before, now, queuing up for adjudication.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This would give us a clear sense of whether the grievance handling process is working as intended.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Second, how can we better assist companies, especially small and medium enterprises, to manage the internal grievance handling process effectively?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many large firms already have HR departments or diversity leads who can manage such cases.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But for smaller organisations, HR may be one person juggling multiple roles or the business owner themselves.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Without clear procedures or adequately trained staff to manage discrimination complaints, employees may be reluctant to raise concerns, either out of fear of retaliation, a perception that nothing will change or concern that a poorly handled process could further strain relationships at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Hence, I would like to ask the Ministry: how will it support firms in developing fair and transparent internal processes for handling grievances on discrimination?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Will there be standard templates or model grievance frameworks provided to guide companies, which many in the House have talked about so I will not belabour on such an approach.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Will TAFEP or Workforce Singapore offer training and certification for HR personnel or line managers in managing discrimination complaints sensitively and fairly?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And how will the Ministry ensure that outcomes of internal grievance handling are properly documented so that employer and employee are protected from misunderstanding or misuse?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Beyond compliance, grievance handling must be done with empathy and professionalism.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It should not be seen as a box-ticking exercise, but as a way to rebuild trust, heal relationships and strengthen the workplace culture.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This includes many start-ups, family-run firms, social enterprises and small contractors.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For example, can these workers still seek recourse through TAFEP or mediation if they experience discrimination?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Will there be a transitional assistance or advisory services to help smaller employers adopt fair practices without the same administrative burden as large firms?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Could the Ministry consider a phased approach or incentives, such as grants or toolkits, to help businesses build fair employment systems over time?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And will there be plans to include these smaller businesses into the legislation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is important that our national commitment to fairness is not dependent on company size.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Every worker, regardless of where they work, should feel protected from discrimination and be treated with dignity and with respect.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That requires culture, requires leadership and requires empathy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our goal must be not just to punish discrimination after it occurs, but to prevent it from taking root.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We can do so by helping employers and workers to recognise unconscious bias, to build inclusive hiring practices and to foster workplaces where diversity is seen as a strength.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In this regard, I am heartened that the tripartite partners of MOM, NTUC and SNEF have consistently worked together to promote fair employment through TAFEP.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The success of this legislation will depend greatly on how well we continue that partnership and how effectively we communicate to both employers and workers that fairness benefits everyone.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It builds trust, it attracts talent and strengthens social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, last January, this House debated the first part of the Workplace Fairness Bill.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In that debate, I shared my personal experience of encountering racial prejudice in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It can happen subtly — during promotion opportunities, or the way performance appraisal is conducted.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Some also occurs through work culture or subconsciously, such as conversing in a foreign language that is not inclusive.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Although not always visible, its effects can be deeply painful and affect a worker's dignity and confidence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That is why the Workplace Fairness Bill is so important.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If all cases continue to be brought to tribunals, workplace relationships could become tense and unhealthy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Therefore, my clarification today focuses on how we can strengthen these first two stages — so that every worker feels protected and safe to speak up, and every employer has a fair way to resolve discrimination issues.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our goal is not merely to penalise discrimination after it occurs, but to prevent it from taking root; so that we can build workplaces that are fair and inclusive for all.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, the two Bills that bring the Workplace Fairness Legislation together marks a significant milestone in Singapore's journey towards a more equitable workplace.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As we implement these Bills, let us focus not only on the enforcement, but also on the education, the empowerment and the empathy, for fairness is not just a rule to be followed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is a value to be lived every day in the workplace.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Perhaps, just one clarification, I am not sure whether Mr Louis Chua supported the Bill because he did not specifically state.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Just a point of clarification – so, you support the Bill?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we have heard a wide spectrum of views from Members.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There have been calls to make the claims process more supportive and favourable to workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the other hand, there are also Members who have expressed the need to strengthen safeguards so that employers are not dragged through claims without merit, to the detriment of workplace harmony and economic progress.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What we can all agree, what we all agreed on is the need to ensure that workplace discrimination disputes are resolved in an amicable and in an expeditious manner.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This Bill seeks to do that through a careful balance of the interests of the various stakeholders to achieve this objective.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This Bill covers the right of individuals who faced workplace discrimination to lodge private claims to obtain redress and closure.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The state enforcement framework was part of the first Bill passed in January this year and it empowers the state to adopt a range of penalties against errant employers, such as issuing directions and imposing financial penalties.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi, Mr Edward Chia, Ms Denise Phua, Mr Shawn Loh, Dr Wan Rizal, Mr Muhaimin Malik and Mr Sharael Taha asked about supporting employers, including SMEs, to put in place grievance handling processes and imposing minimum standards on such processes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Given the diversity of firms, differing HR capabilities and their unique operational considerations, we refrained from being overly prescriptive so that each firm will be able to develop a process which is suited to its needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: TAFEP will support firms with practical resources, such as the Grievance Handling Handbook which will provide sample procedures for employers, including SMEs, to reference.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Chia, Ms Mariam Jaafar and Ms Joan Pereira also spoke about empowering workers to raise grievances without fear of retaliation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked how work pass holders would be protected from having their work pass cancelled for filing a claim for workplace discrimination.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employers who retaliate could be subject to penalties imposed by MOM.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Mr Louis Chua and Ms He Ting Ru's suggestions to allow workers to bypass the mediation and go straight to adjudication in certain circumstances, let me recap the intent of mandatory mediation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mediation allows parties to have open conversations to arrive at a mutually agreeable outcome, tailored to their respective needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Litigation leads to a zero-sum outcome where parties either win or lose, and it should always be a last resort.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our mediators are trained to provide a safe space for parties to share their views honestly and support the parties to come to an amicable agreement amongst themselves.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That said, under circumstances in new sections 36H(2) and 36K(2) of the Act, certain claims may proceed to adjudication without mediation sessions being conducted.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will move on to address Members' comments on the time bars for mediation requests and claims.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi sought clarification on how the time bars will work in certain scenarios, and labour MP and NTUC Secretary-General Mr Ng Chee Meng, Mr Louis Chua and Mr Muhaimin Malik called for flexibility in enforcing the time bars when there are exceptional circumstances.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These time bars represent what tripartite partners agree are reasonable for both employers and employees in different scenarios, including where employers do not give notice of their decisions, but employees have evidence that they were discriminated against.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The time bars are designed to encourage timely filing of valid claims before evidence degrades over time, while also providing reassurance to employers that old claims will not be dredged up many years later.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, the time bars also account for extenuating circumstances.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, the new section 36E(4) of the WFA is intended to give employees who are dismissed when certified pregnant more time to come forward.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM also has the discretion to accept late mediation requests and where there are reasonable grounds to do so, such as when the worker is incapacitated or seriously ill.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This discretion is broad to accommodate various circumstances, and we do not intend to be prescriptive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will monitor the implementation of the time bars and we will make adjustments, where necessary.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I should also add that regardless of which time bar is applicable, the worker is still required to provide prima facie evidence of being discriminate against.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members have also sought clarification on the support for workers in the dispute resolution process, including those who are not union members.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As mentioned by NTUC Secretary-General Mr Ng in his speech earlier, union members can turn to NTUC and their unions for support, every step of the way.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: From the moment a dispute arises, members can turn to unions for assistance, and unions can represent members at mediation and at the ECT hearing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Mr Muhaimin Malik's question, I wish to clarify that PMEs who are unionised can be represented by their unions in mediation and at the ECT.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Next, I move to union members working in companies that are non-unionised.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Gho Sze Kee asked why unions cannot represent their members in non-unionised companies in mediation sessions and ECT hearings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To explain, union representation is premised on mutual recognition and trust between the employer and the union.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is why our laws provide for a process of recognition of a union by the employer.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Notwithstanding this, as mentioned by Mr Ng, NTUC members in non-unionised companies can turn to NTUC's team of industrial relations experts and Tripartite Mediation Advisors for their support and advice on their claims.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Last but not least, workers who are not union members.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Cai Yinzhou, Mr Shawn Loh, Mr Muhaimin Malik and Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked about the support for this group of workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I had mentioned when moving the Bill, TAFEP should be their first port of call when they face workplace discrimination.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Such workers can approach TAFEP for advice and assistance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar suggested that TAFEP help workers understand their rights and options.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: TAFEP will also help them with filing the mediation request as the next step of the claim process.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I am glad that Mr Saktiandi Supaat realises how much resourcing we would have to fundamentally provide TAFEP with.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I believe that in the first Bill, Leader of the Opposition also asked me the same point and I registered that.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Additionally, we note that vulnerable workers may need additional support, such as persons with disabilities, fresh graduates who may not be familiar with the law and employment norms, and low-wage workers with fewer resources, as Ms Elysa Chen, Mr Muhaimin, Ms Denise Phua and Ms He Ting Ru have pointed out.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi and Ms Phua suggested having a friend or an independent advocate accompany the worker in the dispute resolution process.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Beyond this scheme, we will consider how we can help these vulnerable workers to better navigate the dispute resolution framework.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We note Mr Louis Chua's comment on the inherent difficulties for workers to prove workplace discrimination.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have to strike a balance between helping workers seek redress and, at the same time, safeguarding employers from frivolous accusations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, for this reason, a worker alleging workplace discrimination must support his claim with evidence such as documents or oral accounts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Further, under the ECT's judge-led process, the Court will proactively manage the fact-finding process and can direct the employer to disclose relevant documents or information.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Loh has asked about the costs of commencing a workplace discrimination claim.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are still working out the relevant fees for the various stages of the dispute resolution process, but I can share our general approach.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Overall, while fees should be kept affordable so that the dispute resolution process is accessible to genuine claimants, they should also reflect the complexity and the efforts needed to resolve higher value claims and deter frivolous claimants and unnecessary inflation of claims.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi asked why there were claim limits for discriminatory hiring decisions but not for other types of decisions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But I thank Mr Saktiandi and Mr Dennis Tan for their suggestions on quantifying damages arising from discriminatory decisions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We had considered this, and we are still considering it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will work on it during the implementation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We agree with Mr Saktiandi's observation that reinstatement is often not a practical remedy given that the employment relationship would likely have broken down.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: From our experience with wrongful dismissal claims, compensation is generally preferred to reinstatement, precisely for that reason.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Nonetheless, we have provided for reinstatement as a possible remedy, since we do not preclude the possibility that there could be situations where a claimant may desire reinstatement, and the relationship can still be mended.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Mr Loh's question on how the courts would award costs against the parties, this is a matter for the Judge hearing the claim to decide based on the facts of the case.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Judge may consider factors such as the conduct of the parties during the proceedings and the efforts made by the parties at amicable resolution.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi, Mr Cai Yinzhou, Ms Gho Sze Kee, Mr Louis Chua and Dr Wan Rizal called for WFA judgments to be published for transparency.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The point they make is an important one, we agree.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, it is a work in progress, we have to work with the Courts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Shawn Loh also highlighted the risk of an individual publicising a claim in social media even while it is being heard by the Courts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Such an act may contravene the sub judice rule, if it risks prejudicing or interfering with the proceedings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Such individuals may be subject to a fine, imprisonment or both.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Dr Wan Rizal and Mr Cai Yinzhou spoke about naming errant employers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, the first Bill that we passed was on state-led enforcement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Desmond Tan asked whether the ECT's jurisdiction should similarly be expanded for other types of employment disputes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Louis Chua also suggested reviewing the limit for these claims.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not think we should conflate the dispute resolution process for wrongful dismissal and salary disputes, with workplace discrimination disputes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There is an existing process for wrongful dismissal and salary claims above $30,000 to be pursued in the civil Courts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are prepared to consider Mr Tan's proposal, and we would have to discuss this further with our tripartite partners, but I seek Mr Desmond Tan's understanding that this is a discussion for another day.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I have shared earlier, extensive groundwork is needed to prepare both employers and workers for the WFA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In response to Mr Edward Chia, Ms Mariam Jaafar, Mr Dennis Tan and Ms Joan Pereira's questions on educating workers on their claims, MOM, NTUC and TAFEP will do their part to inform workers on the WFA, including what constitutes a legitimate claim and the matters that should be raised in such a claim.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The handbook that I spoke about earlier would complement these efforts by educating workers on their rights and obligations under the WFA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Equally important is the work to put the infrastructure in place before the WFA comes into force.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As Mr Loh and Ms Gho pointed out, the devil is in the implementation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I think, in addition, Mr Loh talked about the road to hell is paved with good intentions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have to make sure that we will not go on that road to hell.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will need to make sure we get it right the first time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we are developing the necessary systems and processes and ensuring sufficient well-trained personnel to support the mediation and adjudication of workplace discrimination claims.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This includes uplifting the capabilities of our mediators and developing the pool of suitably qualified mediators for higher value claims.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On Mr Loh, Mr Saktiandi and Mr Chia's comments again on resourcing the agencies implementing the WFA, I want to assure and reassure Members that we will provide them with the necessary resources to do so.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ensuring their readiness to effectively implement the WFA is our top-most priority.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We also hear Ms Pereira's call to monitor the implementation of the WFA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, MOM conducts regular surveys and reports on fair employment practices, including on discrimination-based dismissals and how they have been resolved.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will extend this work to the implementation of the WFA, and we are studying ways to see how we can augment these monitoring efforts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Gho Sze Kee and Mr Sharael Taha asked if we plan to include small firms with fewer than 25 employees in the scope of the WFA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, to reassure Members, such firms will continue to be subject to the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP), and workers can also approach TAFEP should they encounter workplace discrimination.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Cai Yinzhou and Mr Muhaimin Malik also asked for outsourced workers and platform workers to be included in the WFA in the future.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have said it before, a couple of times, we want to take a sure-footed and prudent approach to implement the WFA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, the WFA focuses on protecting workers in employer-employee relationships.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Nonetheless, as I had shared in the debate on the Workplace Fairness Bill in January, the TGFEP will be updated to clarify that platform operators and corporate service buyers should not discriminate based on non-job-related characteristics.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It has been a long journey since the legislation was first announced, I believe, it was during the National Day Rally in 2021.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I want to take this opportunity to express our deep appreciation and our gratitude to our tripartite partners, NTUC and SNEF, for journeying hand in hand with us to safeguard fair and harmonious workplaces in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But I want to also be clear and like I said, sure-footed, and I also want to humbly put this across to everyone in the House that while this legislation is a new landmark in our journey towards a fair workplace, it is not the end of the journey.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, it is not even the beginning of the end, but the end of a beginning.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I said before that we have only just begun.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The real work starts now, with all of you supporting, as we turn our attention now to the task of implementation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I invite everyone to continue working with us towards this goal.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The nine-storey tower rises from a mound of earth.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step. "Bunga cempaka harum mewangi, Disiram embun di waktu pagi.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This was a significant milestone in our journey towards fair and merit-based workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, it requires firms to have grievance handling processes to promote better communication and amicable resolution of workplace issues.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Third, increasing the range of calibrated enforcement levers to strongly deter against unfair employment practices.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As I had explained to this House when passing the Workplace Fairness Bill, we want to take a sure-footed and prudent approach, to maintain the hard-earned harmony we have today in our workplaces and society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is why the WFA focuses on strengthening protections against the most encountered forms of discrimination, covering more than 95% of all the complaints received by the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We had extensive debates in this House over the scope of the law and how it meets the needs of various stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ultimately, I am glad that the House was in unanimous agreement that the Workplace Fairness Bill passed in January is the right move to ensure that employees and jobseekers in Singapore continue to be assured of fair treatment in the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As mentioned in this House previously, the WFA will be introduced in two Bills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The first Bill covered the substantive rights and obligations under the WFA that I have just summarised, and the second Bill before us pertains to how individuals can make private claims under the Act.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have taken considerable time to work closely with our tripartite partners, the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), the Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF), as well as the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) and the Judiciary, on the multi-faceted processes involved.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I would also like to thank the many stakeholders who gave feedback, ranging from human resources (HR) and legal professionals, to non-governmental organisations as well as members of the public.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have considered your views carefully, and the resulting dispute resolution process strikes a judicious balance between the needs of workers and employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Fundamentally, we aim to provide an amicable, accessible and expeditious dispute resolution process for parties in workplace discrimination claims, while preserving our workplace and social harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will now cover how the Bill will: first, encourage parties to resolve disputes amicably amongst themselves, including through mediation; second, provide more workers with access to an affordable and expeditious forum to adjudicate workplace discrimination claims as a last resort; and third, include safeguards to deter and deal with frivolous claims, so as to ensure a fair and just adjudication process.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Parties are encouraged to resolve disputes amongst themselves, through the firm's internal grievance handling process.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If that is unsuccessful, the individual must attempt mediation, with adjudication only as a last resort.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The first Bill passed in January introduced the requirement for all firms to put in place a grievance handling process for workplace discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This allows employees and employers to settle their differences amicably while preserving the employment relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Notwithstanding this, we are mindful that not every instance of grievance handling within the firm will be successful.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The next step in the dispute resolution process is for parties to attempt mediation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mediation allows parties to have open conversations in a safe space to arrive at a mutually agreeable outcome, tailored to their respective needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have heard feedback that workplace discrimination cases could involve complicated situations that are not as straightforward.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, the mediator managing such disputes would need to be well-trained to facilitate the process sensitively.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We agree with the feedback, and I want to assure Members that the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) will do its utmost to build up the capabilities of our mediators so that they have the requisite skillsets to mediate workplace discrimination disputes fairly and professionally.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have already started the work to uplift the capabilities of mediators at the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM) to prepare for the WFA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, TADM mediators handle a range of employment disputes up to $30,000.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will further strengthen the capabilities of TADM mediators so that they will have the skillsets and the competencies to navigate workplace discrimination claims when the Act comes into force.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These measures I believe are crucial so that the mediation process is robust and effectively resolves disputes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If parties are still unable to come to a resolution amongst themselves after mediation, an individual can commence a workplace discrimination claim at the Employment Claims Tribunals (ECT) or the High Court, as stipulated in the new section 36A.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We want to avoid workers and employers being embroiled in lengthy litigation, often associated with high legal costs for both sides.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have therefore designated the ECT to be the main forum to hear workplace discrimination claims.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This provides more workers with access to an affordable and expeditious dispute resolution forum to seek redress.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The ECT was established in 2017 to hear employment claims up to a claim value of $30,000.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It adopts a judge-led approach with simplified rules and procedures, and legal representation is not allowed.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Parties should find it easier to navigate the ECT's simplified process with the Judge's proactive approach, compared to the process in the Civil Courts that is governed by formal procedural rules and where parties have to take the lead in proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Without the need for lawyers in the ECT, the ECT itself is also more accessible to individuals who might otherwise be unable to pursue legitimate claims due to financial constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With these unique features, the ECT provides a more affordable, expeditious and easier-to-navigate alternative to the Civil Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, most cases at the ECT are resolved within six months, while employment-related cases in the State Courts are resolved within 18 months, about three times more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Judges will actively lead the proceedings by directing parties to speak, asking questions to gather relevant facts, and making it clear when issues raised by parties are out of line and irrelevant.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: After each party has presented their case, the judge will consider all the facts and relevant evidence given by the parties before making the judgment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Overall, this is a far more outcome-oriented and expeditious process.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This mirrors the limit for civil claims heard at the District Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The expansion of the ECT's monetary jurisdiction does not mean that we expect workplace discrimination claims to be of higher value than other employment claims today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Instead, the intent is to allow for the vast majority of workplace discrimination claims to be heard in the ECT.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The higher limit ensures that the majority of workers, including professionals, managers and executives (PMEs) who earn higher salaries, can access the ECT's more affordable and expeditious process for workplace discrimination claims.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Workplace discrimination issues are inherently sensitive and can be socially divisive, especially when they concern matters such as race and religion.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Designating the ECT as the main forum to hear workplace discrimination disputes will provide a less adversarial setting for such claims to be resolved, preserving our workplace and social harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While we have strived to make the dispute resolution process accessible, we recognise that some parties may still require guidance through the process.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First and foremost, TAFEP remains the first port of call for workers and employers who need advice and assistance on workplace discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, TAFEP can guide claimants on the criteria for a WFA claim, direct them to the relevant guides and resources, and outline their options for them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In addition to TAFEP's advice, unions can also help their members – both workers and employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Union representatives can represent parties at mediation sessions and ECT hearings.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Workers may be represented by their union per the status quo for ECT proceedings today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Unionised companies can now also be represented by their unions such as SNEF, for claims between $30,000 and $250,000, and if the worker filing the claim can also be represented.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, in other words, the union for the employers can represent them if it is above $30,000, up to $250,000, but only if the worker filing the claim can be represented.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is a new feature for employers, who currently cannot be represented by their unions in the ECT, as they may need support for higher value claims.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I have outlined how claims up to and including $250,000 will be managed at the ECT.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For higher value claims above $250,000, these are better heard by senior judges on the High Court bench, with legal representation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is also the case for other types of high-value employment claims today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I do not expect many workplace discrimination claims to be commenced in the High Court.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This means that the media or members of the public cannot attend the hearings.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Private forums create a safe environment where parties can share their honest views and focus on the ongoing case, without third parties present who may publicly misrepresent and sensationalise issues, resulting in inflamed social tensions.
