speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Time bars encourage individuals to come forward earlier before the evidence degrades over time and it also provides our employers with some certainty that incidents from the past will not be dredged up years later.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We believe this is a balanced approach as it is practised for other employment disputes and in other jurisdictions as well.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In our public engagements, we heard a concern, particularly from employers and HR professionals, about the risk of frivolous and vexatious claims and of unreasonable inflation of claim values.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To be clear, individuals with genuine cases of workplace discrimination should be able to seek redress.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, frivolous and vexatious claims weaken our workplace harmony and employers should not be burdened by such claims.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Judges will also be empowered to strike out claims on their own motion and can award costs against an individual who pursues a claim that is without merit.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In addition, individuals filing such claims can be investigated by the Police for abusing the Court's processes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If they persist in raising unmeritorious claims, they can be restricted from commencing further legal proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We also heard feedback that with the increase in the ECT's jurisdiction, there is a risk of claim amounts not being pegged appropriately.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Workers may not know how to go about justifying their claim amounts and employers may be concerned about unnecessary inflation of claim values.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM will work with tripartite partners to explore ways to address this in the implementation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Claimants will still need to prove their losses to justify the damages claimed; and judges will also make a fair and balanced assessment of the reasonableness of the claim amount.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When we moved the Workplace Fairness Bill in January this year, I had at the time said that the Act was expected to come into force in 2026 or 2027.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have considered and we have heard feedback from various stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM recognises that ample preparation is critical for successful implementation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employers need to review their HR processes and workers need to know their protections and what constitutes a legitimate discrimination claim.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also need time to ensure our mediators are well trained to effectively facilitate workplace discrimination cases.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the meantime, we will step up our education and outreach efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: TAFEP is working closely with partners, such as SNEF, the Institute for Human Resource Professionals (IHRP), the Singapore Human Resources Institute, and trade associations and chambers, such as the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises, to educate employers on the new legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: TAFEP will also proactively reach out to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to ensure that they are aware of their responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In addition, TAFEP is also designing step-by-step guides and templates that SMEs can easily access, understand and customise for their needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are also resources, such as briefings, clinics, a webpage housing information on fair employment practices and HR e-learning modules that companies can incorporate into their own in-house corporate training, just to name a few.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is just as important that individuals are also aware of their rights and where to seek help.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, we will provide guidance to jobseekers and employees on what matters can be raised as a workplace discrimination claim.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This includes ensuring individuals know where to turn to for help, for instance, within their firm, their unions or to TAFEP.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To make the Act simple to understand and apply, we will also develop a handbook to capture the legal provisions and key principles behind the law, for instance, through illustrations and case studies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: (In Mandarin):   This Second Bill is an important step in implementing the Workplace Fairness Act (WFA).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It outlines how disputes between employers and workers should be resolved fairly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our goal is to create a fairer and more harmonious workplace, maintaining trust between employers and workers while also safeguarding the interests of both.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, we will put in place multiple safeguards to prevent frivolous claims and to ensure the process is fair to law-abiding employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM, together with TAFEP, SNEF and NTUC, will help to prepare the employers and workers for the WFA's implementation at the end of 2027.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, this is a landmark Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Please also allow me to say a few words in Malay.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Please forgive my pronunciation if I get it wrong, but it is very, very important.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: (In Malay):   This Second Bill sets out the process for workers who faced discrimination to seek redress from employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The process encourages employers and workers to resolve disputes among themselves, which helps keep our workplaces harmonious.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Adjudication at the ECT or the High Court should be a last resort.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, the Workplace Fairness Act, as I have shared in the past Bill is not a panacea to resolving workplace discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Notwithstanding, this is a significant step in our ongoing journey towards fairer and more harmonious workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There is no room for discrimination in our workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When such cases unfortunately arise, we want the parties involved to be equipped with the necessary tools and resources which will then allow them to resolve the issue amicably and expeditiously.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In doing so, we aim to preserve, reinforce and improve all of our existing norms on fair and harmonious workplaces for all.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And I declare my interest as the Secretary-General of the NTUC.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: At NTUC, we believe that every worker deserves a fair chance to succeed.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Fairness must rest on skills, performance and potential, and not on personal traits that have no bearing on a person's ability to do a job.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: That is why NTUC has long championed for stronger, clearer and more enforceable protections against workplace discrimination for all workers, including our PMEs who have told us that they want greater assurance of fair and equal opportunity.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For instance, in 2020 to 2021, as part of the SNEF-NTUC PME Taskforce, we spoke with over 10,000 PMEs, employers and stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We heard many stories of workers, especially our mature PMEs over 40, about being passed over due to their age or nationality.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For workers, including PMEs, the process must be fair, accessible and expeditious, while preserving the trust and harmony between workers and employers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: That is why NTUC supports the mediation-first, judge-led approach to resolving workplace fairness disputes under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: A mediation-first process opens the space for workers and employers to understand each other's perspectives and fully explore the possibilities for amicable settlement at the earliest possible stage.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The ECT's judge-led approach will help workers to navigate the claims process, without the need for costly legal representation, which often places the workers at a disadvantaged position vis-à-vis employers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In other words, many workers, including PMEs whose claims are not likely to exceed $250,000, will have access to a tried and tested process to resolve workplace fairness claims fairly and quickly without the need to incur legal costs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This is therefore not only about giving each worker fair recourse, but it is also a clear and trusted system that encourages employers to reflect on their own practices and uphold fairness at every stage of employment.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: When workers know that they can raise issues safely and employers know what fairness requires, workplace culture improves for all.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: At the end of the day, all of us want a fairer Singapore, where workers are valued for their skills and contributions, not penalised for traits that have nothing to do with their workplace performance.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And while firms are required to have fair grievance handling processes, workers want that assurance that they will be treated fairly and protected against retaliation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: So, if you are a union member, you would not have to face this alone.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC and our unions are here to guide you every step of the way – from the moment a dispute arises, through mediation and if needed, all the way to the ECT.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For many years, unions have been quietly supporting our workers, drawing on deep industrial relations experience and established relationships with employers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Around 95% of workplace disputes surfaced to NTUC-affiliated unions are resolved at the company level, avoiding the need for further escalation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Like MOM, NTUC is also stepping up training for our union and NTUC officers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC's Ong Teng Cheong Labour Leadership Institute is working with TAFEP on courses for our union leaders and industrial relations officers to equip them to handle workplace fairness claims.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We are also actively exploring mediation training provided by the Singapore Mediation Centre for our union leaders and industrial relations officers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In addition, we will be looking at how to provide legal support for complex cases.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For NTUC members in non-unionised companies, our staff team of industrial relations experts and Tripartite Mediation Advisors at NTUC stand ready to support and advise you on any claims.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I am glad to hear the Minister's speech about how Government with tripartite partners will plan to see how we can help workers and employers navigate this process.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I had wanted to ask that question, but thanks to Minister Tan See Leng's speech, I have clarity that tripartite partners will follow through with the implementation and up our game in supporting a fair resolution of any disputes.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: But I do have a couple of questions that I would pose to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For workers, I know that the time limits to file claims – while broadly in line with the time-bars for other employment claims today – still can be quite tight.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Workers have one month, six months, and one month respectively to file claims for pre-, in- and end-employment claims.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: AI-based hiring tools could be used for efficiency, but could also unintentionally favour certain groups over others.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I hope that together with tripartite partners, we can study how to ensure that such AI systems are fairly used, transparent and accountable – so that technology helps workers, rather than hinder them.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: (In Mandarin):   NTUC firmly believes that every worker, regardless of age or background, should have fair opportunities for success based on their skills, performance and potential.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This Bill represents an important step forward for us and affirms the crucial role of trade unions in promoting workplace fairness.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our unions have consistently provided quiet assistance to workers facing discrimination.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC and our unions will continue to stand together with workers, providing them with guidance, advice and support when facing challenges.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We also encourage employers to use this opportunity to thoroughly review their company culture and human resource practices, ensuring that fairness and meritocracy are not merely slogans on the wall, but genuinely implemented principles.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We will also work hand in hand with our tripartite partners to collectively build a workplace environment where every worker is valued, respected and has opportunities for growth.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC and our unions are heartened by the progress made, together with our tripartite partners through the Workplace Fairness Act.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: There is still work to be done to shift mindsets, raise HR standards and nurture strong labour-management cooperation, so that fairness becomes part of our workplace culture.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC and our unions will keep working steadfastly with employers and Government to make fairness a lived reality – where every worker is valued for their contribution, treated with dignity and given a fair chance to progress.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I emphasised then that while the Bill was both timely and necessary, it also posed significant questions: whether the scope of protection is adequate, whether access to justice will be meaningful, and whether the reality of power asymmetries in the employment relationship will be sufficiently addressed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Today, we turn our attention to the second Bill on this matter, covering dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: An inclusive and just society demands robust protections against discrimination, not just regulatory compliance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I will address five linked themes: first, a review of claim limits across legislation; second, access to the claims process; third, evidential burden and power imbalance; fourth, transparency and information availability; and fifth, reconsidering the time bars.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Under the Workplace Fairness (Dispute Resolution) Bill, which sets out the grievance-handling process for workplace discrimination claims, parties involved in a workplace discrimination claim must first undergo mediation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Often, discriminatory practices, salary disputes and wrongful dismissal claims are intertwined and point towards poor workplace culture and hiring practices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, I would like to take this opportunity to reiterate the call made in 2016 by WP MPs during the debate on the Employment Claims Bill, for the claim limits for salary and wrongful dismissal claims heard before the ECT to be reviewed and raised, which is all the more pertinent today, given that the claim limits under the ECT are now raised to $250,000 for discrimination.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Next, on ensuring access to the claims process.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The claims process must be accessible to the worker who is already disadvantaged compared to the employer, be it economically or in terms of information and other resources.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Employers are now required to establish an internal grievance process for discrimination claims, and these serve to resolve issues at the ground level and preserve working relationships where possible.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Should these efforts be unsuccessful, parties must attend mediation; currently a mandatory step before adjudication.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The heavy emphasis on mediation for dispute resolution, according to the Tripartite Committee's report, is aimed at preserving workplace harmony and maintaining a non-litigious workplace culture.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, I am concerned that all is not as it seems.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Despite the report highlighting that 94% of employees who lodged salary claims fully recovered their salaries via the TADM and ECT, the fine print also states that the amount agreed between the involved parties during mediation is also considered as the full salary payable, even though this agreement might be reached due to compromise on the part of the claimant, thus resulting in them settling for less on the worry that "something is better than nothing".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, concerns remain about mandatory mediation, especially after employment termination.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Mediation works best when both parties participate in good faith, but claimants may be unwilling or unable to further engage, especially after experiencing psychological distress or toxic environments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Although the Tripartite Committee's report recommended compulsory mediation for both parties prior to the adjudication stage, it also acknowledged that workplace discrimination cases could be challenging to mediate.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This observation is echoed by the Association of Women for Action and Research's (AWARE's) position paper on Discrimination in the Workplace, which highlights that where the claimant suspects that they had been discriminated against, they would prefer seeking redress via adjudication over mediation as they do not wish to settle the matter.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Will the Government reconsider its position or leave the door open on mandatory mediation in future, at least for acute or egregious claims, empowering victims to opt for adjudication instead, if they so choose?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In such cases, the ECT may still retain the option to direct the parties for mediation first, if it believes it to be appropriate, or accept the case and hear the case directly.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My third theme is on the evidential burden.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In employment discrimination claims, the power lies almost invariably with the employer who controls data, documents, HR decisions, appraisals, records, future opportunities, while the employee may have very limited evidence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This structural imbalance demands that the law provide a fairer evidential structure.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Can the Minister clarify the burden of proof and what would constitute sufficient evidence at the ECT, should a claimant wish to file a claim?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is often difficult to prove that an employer's adverse employment decision is due to discrimination on the basis of one's protected characteristic.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, Singapore's employment laws do not require any reason to be furnished when terminating the services of an employee.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Meanwhile, some errant employers may deploy Performance Improvement Plans as a formality despite already being intent on terminating an employee's services.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These actions might obfuscate discrimination beneath a veneer of legitimacy, thus making it harder for claimants to prove their case.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Disabled Persons Association of Singapore put forth that a victim should be required only to establish a prima facie case by adducing facts from which it may be presumed that the employer had discriminated against them.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The burden should then shift to the employer to prove that it did not commit the alleged prohibited action.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have shared in my speech earlier this year, the point about circumstantial evidence is an important one, given the colossal task faced by employees in proving discrimination.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is not easy to detect workplace discrimination as employers would attempt to hide it.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, employers would not indicate in black and white that an employee is being terminated due to their age.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But rather, the employee would perhaps hear it via word-of-mouth from a fellow colleague.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, they might even hear it directly from their line managers, but have no concrete recording of it, allowing him or her to subsequently deny having said such a thing at all.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It would further add insult to injury if the employee were compelled to resign on his or her own accord, at least on paper, when he or she is compelled to do so given the discriminatory workplace environment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, the employee would most likely have, at best, indirect or circumstantial evidence of any wrongdoing by the employer in such cases.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The establishment of a framework for the handling of indirect evidence would be helpful for workers who might be afraid of seeking redress as they feel that they lack substantial evidence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The fourth theme I wish to touch on is transparency and information availability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I respect the Government's emphasis on workplace harmony and confidentiality to safeguard all parties involved, secrecy may also undermine public confidence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One of the requirements regarding workplace discrimination claims is that the claims will be heard in a private setting.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: According to MOM, this provides a private forum for all the parties involved to air their views freely without "worrying that third parties may misrepresent or sensationalise issues in the public domain".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, Court judgments provide an important reference point for prospective claimants to understand from precedent whether their own case holds water.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, it also educates the general public on the types of behaviour that would be unacceptable under these regulations and provides employers with an opportunity to review their own policies and processes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, ECT judgments are not subject to a gag order as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For High Court judgments, while section 36O of the Bill calls for all proceedings held in the High Court under the Workplace Fairness Act to be conducted in private, section 45 of the Bill empowers the General Division of the High Court or the Registrar of the Supreme Court to publish information regarding a judgment pertaining to the Act.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the interest of open justice, I hope that the Government will publish all ECT and High Court judgments pertaining to workplace discrimination cases by default on an anonymised basis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would help enrich the public's understanding of workplace discrimination, while factoring in the need for confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, revealing the company names that are charged under this Bill, as mentioned by Leader of the Opposition Pritam Singh, would help educate employers and the general public about discriminatory workplace practices, whilst sending a strong signal that this is a matter that should be taken seriously.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, an inclusive and just society demands that we do not rest on our laurels but to constantly ensure that dispute resolution mechanisms serve workers fairly and that our laws reflect not merely regulatory compliance but a genuine commitment by all to worker protection.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope the Government can remain open to the refinements posed in my speech as well as those of other colleagues as we work towards a fairer and more equitable employment landscape.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This Bill builds upon the Workplace Fairness Act passed in January this year, a milestone that made workplace discrimination unlawful in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Today's Bill at the second pillar, it sets out how fairness is to be applied and resolved.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It establishes a clear and compassionate process that encourages internal resolution first, followed by mediation and if necessary adjudication at the employment claims tribunals or at the High Court.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Protection and due process now go hand-in-hand, empowering workers to seek redress safely, swiftly and without fear.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: For many workers, especially women, caregivers and those in lower-wage roles, it is deeply personal.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The Act's protected characteristics, including sex, marital status, pregnancy and caregiving responsibilities matter to real people.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Our women workers have written and spoken to me, sharing that even today, bias still shadows their careers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: One woman was asked during an interview, whether she planned to start a family, a question that had nothing to do with the job.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Another, a manager, found her duties reduced when she returned from maternity leave, and a daughter, who took time off to care for her elderly parent told me her performance appraisal never recovered after she returned.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These stories show why the Workplace Fairness Act is necessary.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They send a clear message that no workers should face adverse treatment because of gender, age, or family responsibilities and the law now stands behind them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Yet, Mr Deputy Speaker, while fairness is a noble aspiration, it must be translated into a language and action to mean something for our people.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We must empower our workers to name what feels unjust and to stand up for what is right, especially those who may not yet have the words, knowledge or confidence to do so.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Indeed, the quiet feelings I mentioned, the uneasy thought that one's family plans might have cost a job offer, the sense of being sidelined after having a baby, or the discouragement of seeing targets met but promotions withheld are all very real experiences.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The question is: how do workers give words to these feelings and how do they know when an act of bias becomes true discrimination?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Each number represents a worker who found the courage to speak up and perhaps many more who still remain silent.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: One resident from Punggol told me this: "Ms Yeo, my boss said he wanted younger people, fresh faces.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I do not know how to write and I do not want to cause any trouble." Mr Deputy Speaker, these are not isolated cases.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: For the less resource and less articulate, this provides not just a process, but a safe channel to be heard.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I appreciate that by requiring mediation first and limiting formal legal representation, the Bill levels the playing field.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It prevents David versus Goliath situations where legal resources might otherwise determine the outcome.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Still, many workers may not know how to use these rights.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They may not know how to file a grievance, record evidence or represent themselves before a tribunal and that is where the Labour Movement and now unions, play a vital role.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Unions help workers frame their cases clearly, mediate early before conflicts escalate and provide protection against power imbalances.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This is not her real name, but it is a real person.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: She is a resident and by Punggol constituency and an NTUC union member.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Kelly had just signed an offer for a full-time job when she discovered that she was pregnant.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Out of integrity, she informed her future employer about this.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: She was told that the offer will change to a two-month contract or made part-time instead.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Kelly felt something was wrong but could not quite put it into words.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: With union support, Kelly left the arrangement without penalty and later found meaningful work as an educarer near her home in Punggol.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   This Bill is particularly important for ordinary workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: When many workers face unfair treatment at work, it is not that they do not dare to speak up, but rather they do not know how to articulate their concerns or whom to approach for help.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This is precisely why the role of unions becomes even more critical.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Unions can help workers transform that vague feeling that "something does not seem quite right" into concrete facts and clear language, making their concerns more articulate and well-reasoned.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Unions can also teach workers how to document evidence and how to express themselves during grievance and mediation processes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Through this Bill, workers' voices will carry more weight, and the channels for raising grievances will be safer and clearer.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: When workers know how to express themselves and understand how to exercise the rights that this Bill grants them, fairness will no longer remain merely words on paper, but will become genuine protection that they can truly feel and experience.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: For union members and unionised workplaces, the presence of union leaders and industrial relations officers gives workers courage to come forward and gives employers confidence that matters will be handled fairly and privately.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Through union, branches, tripartite committees, community access to legal clinics and education efforts, we must ensure that every worker, regardless of background or literacy has access to justice at work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I call on the Government to continue to build resources, formal and formal with the tripartite to support our workers through the grievance process.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But I recognise that implementing new requirements can be challenging for smaller companies especially those without HR teams or resources.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Many SME owners have shared with me their concerns that this Bill could open them to frivolous or vexatious complaints, but they remain deeply committed to fairness.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Our SME owners run lean operations, treat staff like family and work side-by-side with their teams.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These mechanisms protect both workers and employers, deterring bad faith claims while preserving trust.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They simply need the tools to do so.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We can support them through HR advisory clinics, templates for fair employment practices and accessible training on inclusive leadership.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Compliance should not feel like a burden and it must not add to already increasing business costs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It should be seen as a good business practice and a high ground for companies to attract and retain a quality workforce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And that is why the NTUC's SME Partners, and Women and Family units have been working with SMEs to build capability and promote gender inclusive workplaces.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Initiatives like the NTUC Better Workplace Programme, which supports wellness and breastfeeding lactation spaces show that fairness can be lived out in everyday ways.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I hope that the Government will continue to provide templates, training and resources to help our SMEs operationalise fairness and to recognise firms that adopt these practices early.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Again, fairness should not be a compliance burden, it should be a shared standard that uplifts both workers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: However, I wish to raise several important questions and concerns regarding the implementation of this dispute resolution framework.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Section 36(i) provides that individuals may be represented by persons prescribed under the regulations made under section 44.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I seek clarification on whether these regulations will mirror the First Schedule of the Employment Claims Regulations 2017.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Under the current framework, trade union members face restrictions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: They cannot be represented during settlement discussions and executive employees have even narrower representation rights.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: While I understand the intent to facilitate direct communication during mediation, we must ask: are these restrictions appropriate for discrimination cases which often involve complex power dynamics and emotional distress?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, I am even more concerned about vulnerable workers who are not trade union members.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Will pro bono channels be expanded to ensure all parties can access legal advice about their rights under the WFA?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, the current regulations only mandate parental representation for those below 18 years of age.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I urge the Ministry to consider extending support to young workers who have just entered the workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Fresh graduates who may be experiencing discrimination but lack the knowledge, resources or union membership to navigate the system effectively, particularly those with less than five years of full-time permanent employment.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: My second point concerns the discretion to extend the time limits under section 36E(4).

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The Bill stipulates that dismissed employees must file for mediation within one month of their last day of employment with special provisions for pregnant employees.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: In such circumstances, one month passes quickly, and by the time they seek help, the deadline has expired.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Section 36F(1A) allows the Commissioner to accept late request if there is a reasonable excuse.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I ask the Minister what constitutes a reasonable excuse.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Will the Commissioner adopt the broader, just and equitable approach found in the United Kingdom's (UK's) Equality Act 2010, which the Employment Appeals Tribunal has interpreted as requiring a wide discretion based on the factual matrix.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: TADM still assisted parties willing to set settle amicably.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: These statistics will help us understand whether the current framework adequately serves workers who may need additional time due to genuine hardship.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: My third point addresses the implementation of grievance handling processes.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Section 36D(2) requires that mediation requests follow internal grievance handling, which section 27 of the WFA mandates employers to establish.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: While tripartite standards and implementation guides exist, I ask how many TADM claims involve employers who lacked proper grievance handling processes.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This data is essential to access compliance and effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: More importantly, have HR professionals in affected companies receive adequate training on these processes?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: What support has the Ministry provided for SMEs which may lack dedicated HR teams?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I urge the Ministry to work closely with SMEs to boost their HR capabilities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Does the Ministry have a roadmap, perhaps over five years to help companies with fewer than 25 employees implement robust grievance handling processes?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Without such support, the dispute resolution framework risks being undermined at its very foundation.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Section 36A limits civil action to alleged discriminatory employment decisions made by employers under section 17(1) of the WFA.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: An employer is defined as a person who employs another under a contract of service.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This excludes workers on contracts for service, platform workers and critically outsourced workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Outsourced workers are among our most vulnerable, often older workers in lower income jobs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Currently, the Tripartite Advisory on Outsourced Workers does not cover anti discriminatory practices by service buyers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This creates a troubling situation where service buyers can specify preferred race, age or religion of the workers, forcing service providers to implement discriminatory practices or face contractual penalties.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: It is unjust to penalise service providers when service buyers are the ones making discriminatory demands.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We are, as the saying goes, barking up the wrong tree.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The UK's Equality Act 2010 addresses this through section 41, which defines contract workers and principals.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: A principal is one who makes work available for individuals employed by another party and contract workers are those supplied in furtherance of such contracts.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This framework effectively extends protection to outsourced workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: How is the Ministry currently educating service buyers on fair employment practices and monitoring discriminatory clauses in service contracts?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Deputy Speaker, the Workplace Fairness (Dispute Resolution) Bill aims to help individuals who face discrimination in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This Bill, together with the Workplace Fairness Act, represents an important step in protecting workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: However, I would like to raise several questions and concerns regarding its implementation.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We need to reconsider some regulatory restrictions placed on workers as they go through this process.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: For workers who are not union members, they will certainly need more support.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, I would also urge that young workers be given more support so that they do not easily suffer discrimination due to lack of experience and knowledge.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, on the issue of time limits and extensions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Typically, they are in desperate situations and they say that the one-month period is too short.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Among other things, I urge that a discretionary approach could be considered in accepting late applications, if there are reasonable grounds.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Third, relating to the implementation of the complaint handling process.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Since employers need to have internal complaints procedures, we need to ensure that HR officers in companies have adequate training.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This is especially important for small and medium enterprises, where their staff may lack the capability to handle the complaint processes properly.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This will ensure fairer employment practices for all categories of workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, the Workplace Fairness (Dispute Resolutions) Bill is a welcome development.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: However, for it to truly deliver justice, we must ensure that vulnerable workers can access representation, that time limits accommodate genuine hardships, that employers, especially SMEs, have the capacity to implement proper processes, and that our most vulnerable workers, including those outsourced, are not left behind.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I call on the Ministry to address these concerns so that the promise of the workplace fairness becomes a reality for all workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, this Bill is a landmark legislation towards creating fairer and more equitable workplaces.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I stand in support of this Bill and offer three points for consideration.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While union members in non-unionised companies have access to Tripartite Mediation Advisers, a proportion may not and may struggle to understand the discrimination and the experiences or articulate the details of unfair treatment.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister clarify specific resources to support non-unionised workers through the ECT procedures?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, I understand the position that Court proceedings would generally be held in private to foster open discussions without public misrepresentation.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, there is significant public interest in serious workplace discrimination cases and to hold employers accountable, the current Bill appears to offer limited discretion for the High Court to publish this information.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, I note that this Bill does not amend the scope of the Workplace Fairness Act, which excludes outsourced workers and freelancers, including platform workers.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the enhanced Bill comes into force, I look forward to seeing the Ministry reviewing these aspects of expanding protections to outsourced workers and freelancers.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I commend the Government and congratulate all stakeholders, including NTUC, TAFEP and SNEF for their efforts in bringing this Bill and its dispute resolution mechanisms to fruition.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Bill is a tripartite win, demonstrating the collaborators' spirit of employers, unions and the Government in establishing clear roles and a robust framework for workplace fairness.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Notwithstanding these three clarifications, Deputy Speaker, Sir, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: An unfair dismissal or discrimination could well be part of the factual matrix in some cases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I also suggested for one tribunal to hear all types of labour disputes, including employment claims and claims for unfair dismissal and discrimination.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Today, I am happy to support and welcome this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is a welcome development, especially in the context of our ageing population and changing social landscape which puts the spotlight on fair employment practices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, as with many new frameworks, the true test of its effectiveness will lie in how it works in practice where ordinary workers can navigate the process and whether smaller employers can comply without being unduly burdened.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is therefore important that the Bill's implementation is accessible, balanced and workable for all parties involved.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, for many lower-income or less educated workers or employees, they may still not be aware that they have such rights or may be intimidated by the process of filing a claim, as it is often not just the information itself, but the practical process that is challenging.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Understanding what happens next, for example, what to expect after filing a claim, what documents to bring, or how to respond during mediation can be intimidating for those unfamiliar with formal dispute processes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will there be any public education efforts in vernacular languages to ensure that low-wage workers are also aware of their rights pertaining to workplace discrimination and recourse available to them as outlined in this Bill?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will there be practical step-by-step support available, such as assistance with completing claim forms or responding to procedural queries, for workers who may lack the literacy or confidence to file a claim?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For instance, the Community Justice Centre currently provides volunteers to assist litigants in person in our Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A similar scheme could perhaps be adapted for TADM mediations to ensure that workers who need it can receive practical guidance and reassurance throughout the process.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Lay people are often not comfortable, even with say, the need to file sworn evidence to start the claims.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, in this connection, I urge the Government to continue to work towards simplifying claims procedure for lay people across different applications, including for the discrimination claims at ECT or in the High Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, I would like to seek clarification in respect of work-pass holders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If so, should we be concerned that employers have the ability to cancel work passes and repatriate their employees upon termination of employment before or in the midst of their pursuing or initiating a claim, and they may not be able to remain in Singapore to attend mediation or hearings, weakening the practical effect of the protections offered under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Employers should, of course, not be penalised for unsuccessful claims.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, they should not be responsible for employees' additional expenses resulting from the unsuccessful claims, including expenses for prolonged stay in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many SMEs operate on lean manpower and limited administrative support.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even though the system is designed to be a lawyer-free process at ECT level, the reality is that such an employer still needs to gather facts, compile documentation and prepare explanations to defend its case.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A small enterprise with, say, 25 to 30 employees, for example, is unlikely they have the HR or legal support that a larger company can afford.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given that this Bill introduces new procedural requirement obligations and the possibility of claims being lodged against employers, how can it be ensured that smaller enterprises are not overwhelmed by the process?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What kind of clear guidance or advisory support will be given for SMEs to understand the process and their responsibilities?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is not to discourage legitimate complaints, as every genuine claim should be heard fairly, but the system should also ensure that smaller employers are protected from disproportionate strain.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, accountability through transparency and prevention of repeat offenders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Well, Mr Deputy Speaker, while confidentiality for employees and employers must be respected, complete opacity also limits public learning and deterrence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A people-centred balance will be to keep case details confidential, but at the very least require the publication of anonymised aggregated outcomes and quarterly data.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such data, for instance, the number of cases by sector, the types of discrimination alleged and their outcomes, would help identify trends and systemic issues.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If certain sectors consistently show higher proportions of age-related or gender-related claims, the Ministry can then target outreach training or policy interventions more effectively.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Beyond transparency, data can also strengthen accountability by helping to detect repeat offenders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There is room to build on this by establishing a more systematic internal process to monitor and flag repeated breaches by rogue employers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This would enable earlier intervention and signal that the framework is responsive to patterns of behaviour, not just individual disputes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It can also help to study undesirable practices or behaviour on the part of errant employers, or even employees, which MOM can use to consider improvements and revisions to prevailing laws.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Ultimately, Mr Deputy Speaker, the true measure of workplace fairness lies not only in the number of disputes resolved, but in how many are prevented by embedding a capacity for early intervention within this framework.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We make fairness not just a recourse, but a shared habit woven into the daily life of our workplaces and the moral fabric of our economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Bill has provided for the jurisdictional limits of discrimination claims between the ECT and the High Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, can losses such as injury to feelings be claimable and if so, how will such claims be quantified?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Government's answers can provide helpful and important preliminary guidance and reference via the Hansard for the implementation of the new law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the typical quantum of claims arrived by the ECT and the High Court for the new tort will be reasonable for both employers and employees, so that there will be fairness for both employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, this Workplace Fairness Bill, together with existing regulations, allows employees to seek mediation with their employers or lodge complaints with arbitration bodies when they encounter unfair treatment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Whether they are discriminated against due to age, gender, pregnancy, childbirth, marital status, caregiving responsibilities, nationality, race, religion, language ability or disability, or are wrongfully dismissed, employees can protect their rights according to law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, having rights does not mean everyone can exercise those rights.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For some employees with lower income or education levels, they may not even know they have such rights.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even if they know, they may not dare to, not know how to, or where to start.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even if they have heard about it, they might think: "Aiya, these procedures are so complicated, I cannot explain clearly, and I do not understand those forms." Some people will be afraid – afraid of saying the wrong thing, afraid of offending their boss, afraid of trouble.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As a result, even when they are in the right, they dare not speak up; even when they have grievances, they dare not seek redress.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Third, will practical assistance be provided to employees with lower education levels, such as teaching them how to fill out forms, prepare documents and answering procedural questions, helping workers with weaker literacy skills or less confidence to take that first step steadily?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even though these procedures are already simpler than ordinary Court processes, they still pose challenges for ordinary people.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Therefore, I hope the Government, when implementing this Bill, will not overlook these practical difficulties.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Make the complaint procedures as easy to understand as possible, so that employees who are not very familiar with or not very good at writing English can smoothly complete the process.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To ensure its success, the key is that we must be committed to ensuring that employees are willing, able and can make use of it, whilst employers can afford it and society can trust in its fairness.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, in conclusion, the Workplace Fairness Bill represents an important move towards fairness at work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To ensure its success, we must focus on making the process accessible to ordinary workers and manageable for small employers while maintaining the confidence of all stakeholders through transparency and fairness.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I look forward to the Minister's clarifications on the questions I have raised.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Notwithstanding the questions and concerns I have raised.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is what every Singaporean hopes for – when they look for a new job, when they ask for a promotion, or when they return from maternity or hospitalisation leave.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I rise in strong support of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When this House passed the Workplace Fairness Bill in the last term, it was a milestone in our tripartite journey.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It affirmed a simple truth that every worker in Singapore deserves to be judged on their ability, not their age, gender, caregiving responsibility, nationality, race or religion.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But principles mean little if people do not know how to seek redress when those principles are violated.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Bill turns principle into practice, giving both workers and employers a clear, fair and accessible way to resolve disputes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But Mr Deputy Speaker, the true test of fairness is not only in how the law is written, or how processes are set up.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is in how workers experience it every day.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Fairness must not only be fair but must feel fair to the people who live it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In my maiden speech in this House in 2020, I spoke of residents I met in my first months on the ground in Woodlands: the 50-something PMET was told he was overqualified, the 40-something banker who watched a foreigner take his job, the 30-something Malay accounts clerk who finds that job ads ask for Mandarin speakers only, the 20-something graduate who gets low-ball offers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Just last night, a resident came to my MPS for help.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She had been terminated with notice, just after returning from hospitalisation leave for in-vitro fertilisation treatment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Employers too, especially SME bosses, have shared their worries that one wrong move or one problem-hire could land them in trouble, even as they face real economic pressure and constant policy changes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In contrast, the formal Employment Tribunal system, where 100,000 claims are filed yearly, is slow with a one year wait time, costly and legalistic.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It keeps trust at the centre of justice and allows employees to pursue claims without the need for legal representation if filed under the ECT.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But mediation must be real and not ritual.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, mediators must first be professionally trained in employment law, discrimination claims and cross-cultural communication, and they must reflect the diversity of our workforce.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Seeking redress is already intimidating, as the burden of proof often rests on the worker.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The same Woodlands resident I mentioned earlier told me that the mediator she spoke to said she could be liable for the entire claim amount if she pursued it at the ECT.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That is not quite what the law provides, so she might have been misunderstood.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But you see how even the perception of risk can chill a worker into silence.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must therefore work to make the process clearer for workers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: MOM and TAFEP can provide plain-language templates, sample grievance letters, timelines, Frequently Asked Questions, so that even an elderly auntie cleaning tables at the coffee shop can navigate the process confidently.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Workers could also be given confidential pre-mediation advisory, where they can understand their rights and options, through TAFEP or trained resources in the community, so that workers who are unsure or afraid have safe, local places to seek advice before taking action.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And crucially, workers must feel protected from retaliatory actions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Bill rightly prohibits retaliation – but in practice, fear of retaliation remains the biggest reason people stay silent.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Could the Minister clarify how retaliatory action claims will be processed under the Workplace Fairness Bill?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We should have strong retaliatory protections, so that fairness is not only about the right to be treated fairly, but also the confidence that if you stand up for that right, you will not stand alone.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many want to comply, but run without HR departments.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: MOM could issue sector-specific starter kits – one-page grievances procedures for retail, food and beverage, logistics, care services and other key sectors in multiple languages.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And a short certification course for SME supervisors on workplace fairness, grievance handling and mediation would also help, so they know what "doing the right thing" looks like in real life.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And for firms that exemplify fairness, we can create a "Fair Employer Mark", recognising companies that lead by example.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because compliance by fear is fragile; compliance by pride is lasting.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Bill rightly channels most cases to the ECT, keeping the process proportionate.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But in the initial years, we should review outcomes through a tripartite monitoring panel to check if cases are rising for the right reasons, and to spot sectors where culture, not law, is the root issue.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That allows us to adjust early before disillusionment sets in.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Bill rightly protects against discrimination on many important protected characteristics.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But there are still Singaporeans who may not see themselves reflected in it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Let us evolve protection as our workforce evolves – steady, consultative, but unafraid to broaden the circle of inclusion.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Fairness must live in the daily decisions of our workplaces – who we hire, how we train, how we promote, how we treat one another.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many Singaporeans tell me, "I do not mind working hard.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I just want a fair chance." That, Mr Deputy Speaker, is what this Bill helps secure – a fair chance for every worker to show their worth and a clear process when they feel otherwise.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must keep building workplaces where Singaporeans feel seen, valued and given room to grow; not passed over, not second-guessed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must keep them engaged in their work, because fairness is not only about protection, it is about participation – giving our people the confidence to stay in the workforce, reskill and take on the next challenge.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because fairness is not a compliance function, it is a leadership habit.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And when employers model that habit, they earn something no law can command: the loyalty and trust of their workers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And it says to every employer – you will be treated fairly and and given a clear process when disputes arise.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That balance between protection and partnership is what has made Singapore work.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we can keep that balance strong, then every Singaporean, whatever their background, can look at this system and say, "it is fair, and it works for me." That is the promise we renew today.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, I would like to raise several issues that we should consider to ensure that the path to justice is kept accessible to all workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, there usually exists a great imbalance between the employer and employee when it comes to employment disputes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While it is encouraging that both parties cannot have external legal representatives before the ECT, this may not be sufficient to level the playing field, especially, as some employers may have legally trained in house legal teams who would be appointed to represent the company.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this regard, I note that there appears to be no legal clinic focused on workers' rights or employment law.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Notably, while the NTUC runs a Law Works Legal Clinic for Union members, the Pro Bono SG website appears to state that this legal clinic excludes employment issues.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Ministry should also continuously work with civil society and community organisations to ensure that workers are empowered to obtain justice under the Workplace Fairness Act through initiatives like education and awareness campaigns, the development of guidance materials and pro bono referral schemes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, I appreciate the importance for proceedings under the Act, including mediation and ECT hearings to be conducted in private in the interest of workplace harmony.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, as mediation and hearings are formal processes, they will undoubtedly be daunting for workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It would thus be particularly nerve wracking for a worker to journey through this process alone.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If so, can the Minister confirm if this will be set out in the regulations or guidelines as to who can serve as support persons and proceedings under the Act?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Third, like my colleague, MP for Hougang, Mr Dennis Tan, I would like to ask that the Minister also clarify about the support available to workers who struggle to navigate the various proceedings because they are not so conversant in English or struggle with digital literacy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such support should at the very least include help to submit claims, file documents and genuinely navigate the procedural parts of the entire process.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: All of us have seen residents who find it particularly challenging to commence claims or to continue pursuing claims through the tribunals, because they are either unable to or lack confidence in navigating the system, and this is particularly important since legal representation is not allowed in ECT proceedings.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Four, there are three particular groups of workers whom we should pay particular attention to, in relation to the dispute resolution mechanisms: one, workers with disabilities; two, workers who have suffered both workplace discrimination and workplace harassment; and three, workers who have been traumatised by their workplace experiences.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On workers with disabilities, the dispute resolution mechanisms should be accessible for different types of disabilities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As it currently stands, the SG Courts website contains an accessibility statement stating that a sign language interpreter may be requested only in certain types of cases.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This should be expanded to include employment cases before the ECT.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also not clear whether claimants who are blind or who have low vision will be able to effectively use the Community Justice and Tribunals System (CJTS), to file and manage their claims under this Act.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Can the Minister confirm that accommodations will be made to workers with disabilities at all stages of the dispute resolution process, when they make a claim under this Act, on workers who have suffered both workplace discrimination and workplace harassment?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The current framework could create unnecessary barriers as they attempt to seek justice.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, they must file a claim with the ECT in respect of the discrimination they have experienced.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Then they must file a separate claim with the Protection from Harassment Court in respect of the harassment they have been subject to.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This imposes another layer for those seeking redress to navigate and may deter a worker from seeking recourse.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This, in turn, may contribute to under reporting and allow errant employers to get away with their bad behaviour because workers are not able or willing to meaningfully engage with the legal process.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One, the requirement for mandatory mediation may unnecessarily risk the re-traumatisation of the worker and cause more harm.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: ECT, tribunal members and judges should be provided with training and support so that they can conduct the dispute resolution process in a trauma informed manner to minimise inflicting further harm on the aggrieved worker who is navigating a complicated legal process to seek justice.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this regard, it is also important that they receive sensitivity training that helps them to understand the lived experiences of workers with the different protected characteristics, so that they can make meaningful and fair decisions.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Making the law is, of course, very different from practising the law.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: When we make laws, we should always consider the broader intent and spirit of the law and how it will be implemented and used.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We also have to consider the implications for our society and the lived experience of those it will touch.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It especially matters for this Bill, since it will guide us on how sensitive matters involving race, language and religion are dealt with in our workplaces.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We mean for our workplaces to be harmonious, non-litigious and for disputes to be settled without escalation as much as possible.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The proposed process is designed to reflect this intent.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I agree that adjudication should be the last resort for any workplace discrimination disputes.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I also think we should not become an overly litigious society.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Not every issue should be fought in Court and not every grievance should be escalated into a legal arms race.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In fact, I advocate for mediation whenever I can in my professional capacity.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Justice is best served when it is quick, fair and accessible.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: And of course, it helps very much if it can be cheap, too, because lawyers can be very expensive.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The ECT was designed precisely for all of that.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I welcome the expanded role and scope that this Bill will give.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There were some concerns about the lack of direct legal representation at the ECTs.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It was pointed out that this may result in an asymmetry of power between the parties for WFA claims, especially so when some companies do have in-house counsels.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: First, I must note that even though direct legal representation is not allowed, there is nothing to stop either side from engaging lawyers to advise and prepare their case.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The same scope for legal professionals that exist under the ECTs still exists.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The intent of the ECT is to deliver adjudication in a fair, quick and accessible way.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Allowing direct legal representation makes it more expensive and it will likely make the whole process more adversarial and dragged out more than it has to be.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This runs contrary to the intent of the ECT.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Furthermore, I imagine if an employer is big enough to have an in-house counsel, then clearly there is already a stark and wide asymmetry of power – a David and Goliath situation.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Allowing legal representation will not do much to alter this inherent imbalance but it will add another layer of cost to both sides, particularly for David.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In a real legal arms race, the pockets of David will hurt far more.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is also less clear in real life who is David and who is Goliath.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We can imagine a small company being disadvantaged by a sophisticated claimant.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But I do believe that in-house counsels could be a problem.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In fact, I did highlight this issue to the Ministry earlier in my capacity as a member of the Government Parliamentary Committee and suggested that in-house counsels should be restricted at the ECT.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: True, we typically see in-house counsels only in larger organisations.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: So, this issue may exist only in a minority of cases, but justice and fairness must not only be done, but it also needs to be seen to be done.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Parties coming through the system must have confidence that they are not handicapped, and that the system is fair and equitable to all parties.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: More than just optics, I also speak from experience.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I know what the capable ones can do.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Allowing them to directly represent companies in the ECT would almost certainly prejudice the employee and lead to unfairness.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There are many ways to define the scope of in-house counsels and specifically exclude them.
