speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: A regulation to that effect could be made by the Minister.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I urge the Minister to consider this point again.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The reason for doing this does not sit well.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There are many laws in place that all employers, big and small, are expected to comply with, including the Workplace Safety and Health Act, the Personal Data Protection Act, the Employment Act, and so on.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, I can see no reason why we should assume smaller firms will struggle with compliance, and why they will need more time than bigger ones.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I cannot find the exact numbers but considering that SMEs make up the overwhelming bulk of companies in Singapore, I think it is safe to assume that these smaller firms make up a significant percentage of employers.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I am glad to see a pathway for unions to directly represent the parties at the ECT.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They will be invaluable in representing the interests of the parties without the added baggage and cost of lawyers.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Direct union representation can happen only if the company and employee are members of their respective unions and the company itself is unionised.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Union members cannot tap on their union to represent them if their company is not unionised.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This strikes me as an odd segregation of union members.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Many working in such capacities are employed by non-unionised companies.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This arrangement leaves out a very significant segment of our workforce.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The people derive their trust from their lived experience with the system.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The process and implementation of this Bill will matter as much as the Bill itself.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I mentioned at the beginning of my speech I always advocate for mediation as a first resort in my professional capacity.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I have much faith in mediation, in a large part because I was fortunate to have worked with many excellent mediators.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I feel that mediation still remains meaningful because it focuses more on resolution rather than reconciliation.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Even after someone leaves a toxic workplace, mediation provides a very natural platform to clarify issues, address lingering grievances and negotiating matters like payment.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It helps both parties move forward without the weight of conflict.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In short, mediation after employment is not about repairing the past.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is also about creating a respectful closure for the future.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: At the end of the day, I would like to say this: the proof of this particular pudding is not in the pudding itself, but in the eating.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The real test only comes when the first cases go through the process prescribed by this Bill.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: And I will be watching the process very closely.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It tells us what should not be done and sets out what happens if it is done.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But we must remember that the law we make is not an end in itself, but only a means to an end.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Ideally, the law succeeds when it never has to be used to punish or correct.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must remember that what we really want in our society is not more claims or more cases.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We do not want to punish what is wrong, but promote what is right.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We want fairness to become second nature in our workplaces.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We want respect, inclusion and equality to become embedded in the work culture here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: And this is what we aspire to see.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: To get there, we cannot rely on legislation alone.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The Ministry, our unions, our employers and our workers.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Only we can make this happen and let us not forget that.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I understand, Mr Dennis Tan, you have a clarification of a Member that has spoken before you?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: At the beginning of my speech just now, I did not make a declaration.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Can I make a very quick declaration now?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is an important step towards making our workplaces fair for every worker.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The process of seeking redress must not only be fair, but also feel safe, especially for those going through difficult life circumstances or personal challenges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Every worker deserves to feel that if something goes wrong, the system will hear them not haunt them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And for union members, we will go further – we will assist them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As part of the NTUC family, I see daily how fairness at work changes lives, from jobseekers rebuilding confidence after rejection, to workers finding understanding employers who give them a second chance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For these workers, fairness is not an abstract principle.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Most who stayed silent cited fear of being marginalised or harming their careers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And that is why this Bill is important.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It assures both workers and jobseekers that redress can be sought safely and confidentially and of course, fairly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They must know that they will be heard without fear of retaliation and that their dignity will be protected.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Take for example a worker who feels sidelined after returning from maternity leave, uncertain if raising her concerns will affect her standing at work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Under this Bill, she can first raise the matter through her company's grievance process.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If unresolved, she can turn to mediation at the TADM and if necessary, to the ECT.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If she is a union member in a unionised company, her union can support her at every step of the journey, even to represent her at the ECT.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Each step is designed to be fair, affordable and private – helping both sides find resolution without hostility or fear.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This protection is for all workers regardless of ability or disability, including those managing mental health conditions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For them, assurances on confidentiality and empathy are especially important.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And for those who are union members, our unions stand ready to walk with them through mediation, to represent them if needed and to ensure their voices are heard with dignity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Consider a jobseeker who discovers that a potential employer withdrew an interview after learning her age or disability.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Under this Bill, she too can bring her case to TADM and if unresolved, to the ECT for resolution.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If she is a union member, NTUC will be on hand to support her during her negotiations with the company, the mediation process and even at the ECT.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This ensures that fairness begins not only in the workplace, but from the very start of one's employment journey.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These examples remind us that fairness is not just a concept, it is a process that protects dignity and trust, whether a person is seeking work or already working.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Even with good laws, fairness is ultimately delivered by people.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Frontline officers, mediators and tribunal staff must be trained to handle cases with care and empathy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our union leaders and industrial relations officers have deep experience in handling workplace disputes and will also go further, training to be equipped to handle workplace fairness cases so that they can recognise distress, manage sensitive conversations and uphold confidentiality in every interaction.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A fair system must not only be efficient but also humane.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This protects confidentiality, reduces reputational harm and ensures sensitive disputes can be resolved respectfully away from the public glare.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This balanced approach protects individual dignity while maintaining public confidence in the system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Workers and the public alike must have confidence that serious misconduct will not be hidden behind closed doors.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I have three clarifications to ask from the Minister.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, a common query I have heard is how the claims amounts will be determined.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Will the Ministry be providing guidelines so that workers and employers will know what to expect when faced with a claim?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, while it is important for ECT proceedings to remain private, published judgments are useful to provide guidance to workers and employers alike on what to expect from claims.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Will the Ministry consider publishing ECT judgments on an anonymised basis?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, even with judges playing an active role in ECT proceedings, it can be very daunting and challenging for workers, especially those who are less educated, to understand what is going on.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While NTUC and our unions will play our part for all our members, what more can be done to assist and guide claimants who need more help?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It should begin in the way we treat each other every day.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The best dispute resolution system is one that workers rarely need to use, because trust and understanding are built early.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our unions work hard to ensure employers have fair workplace practices and grievance handling processes in place, as this builds confidence amongst managers to administer employment, promotion and training decisions meritoriously; and transparency and mutual trust in how grievances are to be handled respectfully.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When employers take steps to handle grievances promptly and respectfully, conflicts can be settled before they even escalate.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When these systems are clear and trusted, workers feel safe to raise issues early and managers gain confidence in addressing them calmly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Employers and employees should also be encouraged to discuss adjustments or concerns constructively, especially when workers have unique needs or face new challenges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Such understanding does more than promote inclusion, it prevents misunderstanding and mistrust, because when workplaces are empathetic, transparent and fair, issues are resolved through conversation and not through confrontation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is how we move from compliance to culture, from managing disputes to preventing them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is truly a Bill that is pro-worker, pro-employer and pro-Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, we often speak about fairness in the workplace.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We know that when discrimination occurs, it is not only the individual who is affected, but the entire community feels the impact.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For workers who lack the confidence to lodge complaints or do not know how to begin the process, I encourage them to become NTUC members.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: NTUC will guide and walk with them throughout the journey of seeking fairness — so that no worker feels alone in facing workplace challenges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is why the spirit of this law is important, not only to protect workers' rights, but to strengthen unity and harmony in our multiracial and multi-religious society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When we act fairly, we are actually preserving Singapore's core values: trust, cohesion and shared hope.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Every action based on empathy and compassion, however small, contributes to the peace and harmony of our nation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, fairness at work strengthens the very fabric of our society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It shows how tripartism turns values into action, and how fairness, when practised with empathy, becomes a shared strength.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Fairness that is not only written in law but lived out in every workplace and in every act of respect between us.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For many, the Bill's greatest gift is clarity and a structured, state-supported initial pathway for dispute resolution.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The anti-retaliation clause and the focus on mediation are foundational steps that can genuinely encourage more individuals to step forward.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The proposed law, while empowering in theory, however, does pose significant challenges for employees who are vulnerable; such as those with disabilities, those who are of advanced age, or with low education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are challenges that could prevent some of these vulnerable employees or potential employees from accessing its protections.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For the law to be truly effective, it must be made accessible, enforceable and empathetic.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Under this Bill, the grievance system may be complex and inaccessible for some.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Vulnerable employees may struggle to navigate procedures, articulate complaints, or understand their rights, creating a gap between the law's existence and its practical use.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The ECT is meant to be simple and accessible but still remains a legal forum.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For many, handling their own cases is unrealistic.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Tasks such as preparing claims, collecting evidence, digital or otherwise, conducting cross-examinations can be overwhelming for those without legal knowledge or digital skills.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Vulnerable workers who lack independent advice are at a clear disadvantage.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They may feel compelled to accept unfair settlements or give up valid claims because the process feels too difficult or intimidating.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is the employee's responsibility to prove that discrimination occurred.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is often quite difficult, especially for vulnerable workers who may not have the resources or skills to collect evidence – such as emails or witness statements – when facing a well-resourced, more resourced employer.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, let me propose four pillars for improvement, for a truly accessible Workplace Fairness Act.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Pillar 1: simplify the path – make the grievance process truly accessible.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, the grievance process remains a maze of complex forms and legalistic language.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For a vulnerable worker, this maze can feel like a solid wall standing in the way of justice.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We must tear down this wall and make the path to redress more accessible.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To do so, employers should be required to provide grievance procedures written in plain and simple language and made available in needed multiple languages and accessible formats – including large print, braille, and audio versions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: MOM and TAFEP should also work together to design clear, user-friendly complaint forms and visual flowcharts that guide workers step by step, helping them answer a fundamental question: "Have I been treated unfairly, and what should I do next?" By simplifying the process, we can transform what is now an intimidating and legalistic system into one that is clear, compassionate, and navigable – empowering every worker, especially the most vulnerable, to take that first step towards fairness and dignity with confidence.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Pillar 2 for improvement: empower the voice – introduce an "Appropriate Adult" scheme in the process.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: No vulnerable worker should ever have to face their employer alone in a formal setting.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The imbalance of power in such situations can silence even the most legitimate claims.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We must give them a voice and ensure that their dignity and rights are protected throughout the process.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This advocate, modelled after the successful "Appropriate Adult" scheme in the UK and in a sense, also implemented already in Singapore for the disabled could be a union officer, a social worker, or disability specialist equipped to support the worker appropriately.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The advocate's role is not to speak on behalf of the worker, but to ensure that the worker is heard.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The advocate helps prevent coercion, translate complex language and provide emotional and procedural support.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In doing so, we balance the scales of power and make the process fairer, more humane and more inclusive for all.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Pillar 3 for improvement: mandate inclusion – legislate the duty for reasonable accommodation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Yet today, the burden still falls on the employee to request reasonable accommodation – and for many, that very burden becomes the barrier that excludes them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Open Door Fund, for example – now the Open Door Programme – was established as early as 2007.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many employers have already demonstrated what inclusion in action looks like.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At the Art Bar, a collaboration with Starbucks, two employees with autism, Salihin and Caleb, have worked as skilled baristas for almost a decade.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Clear signage, visual support, structured routines help them carry out their tasks confidently and independently.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some of you here, including our Senior Minister, was already a customer had witnessed their skills.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Another example, Siew Leng, who is deaf and blind, has been with her organisation SG Enable for over 12 years.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: She uses a refreshable braille display to read documents and emails, and her colleagues assist with phone calls when needed.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These same accommodations enable her to remain productive and valued.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Employers should also be guided by a clear, illustrative list of accommodations: for a wheelchair user, not just a ramp, but also an adjustable desk; for a worker with visual impairment, screen-reading software and braille safety signs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: By legislating this duty, we move the workplace culture from a defensive "Why should I?" to a collaborative "How can we?" – unlocking the full potential of our diverse and capable workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Lastly, Pillar 4 for improvement: prevent harm – conduct proactive fairness audits.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These audits should look at how employees are hired, promoted, retained and developed across groups such as age, gender and disability, and publish anonymised findings.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The purpose of this is to build a culture of transparency and trust, not fear.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It helps companies spot and correct hidden biases early, so disputes become a last resort instead of the only way to seek fairness.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It shifts our approach from punishing unfairness to building fairness right from the start.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, Bill does not fully level the playing field; it merely provides a better-defined one on which the inherent disadvantages of the vulnerable employee still play out.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The journey from experiencing discrimination to securing redress is a marathon.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The system, while improved, still places a significant onus on the individual to navigate complex processes against a typically well-resourced opponent.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The ultimate success of this Bill for Singapore's most vulnerable workers will therefore depend not just on the letter of the law, but on the ecosystem that supports it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This includes robust funding for truly accessible legal aid and support such as the Appropriate Adult scheme, community outreach programmes to educate workers on their rights and the importance of documentation, and ongoing training for mediators and even judges to identify and protect against power imbalances.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Without these complementary measures, the Bill risks being a well-intentioned channel that only the most resilient and resourceful vulnerable employees can successfully pass through.
